focusDirective: what a general explorer can do about runs whose planned faults and client operations can no longer progress: release at the stall, fault timing into the restart-and-delivery window, remaining inert paths

hypothesis.title: At a stall, settle the in-progress client operations for dependency purposes and release the planned events they block, ending at plan completion or the next stall
hypothesis.description: On the stall cap's treated runs, half (a salt of its own; tag STALL_RELEASE = 1 << 12, bit 4096, the retired recoverWindowFreshOnly row renamed stallRelease) do not end at their first stall. Instead exec_plan (path.rs) marks every planned client operation still in `in_progress` as completed in the PlanEngine (engine.mark_event_completed on its plan node) while leaving it in `in_progress` so a late Response is still recorded and cannot double-complete; the write-chain successors, density-edge successors (including crash/recover and partition/heal pairs ordered after the stuck operation) become Ready and issue on the next steps. The release is itself a progress mark, re-arming the clock. The run then ends by plan completion, which is now reachable, or at its next stall as the parent does. Counters: stall_release.releases (runs released), stall_release.ops_settled, stall_release.dependents_released.{client,fault,other}, stall_release.late_responses (a Response after settlement: the operation was slow, not stuck), stall_release.plan_completed_after_release, stall_release.second_stall_stops, stall_release.steps_after_release_sum.
hypothesis.rationale: Baseline: planned_events_outstanding_sum 3,361,713 over 606,180 runs (5.5 per run; 6.4 per unfinished run among the 374,882 runs that recovered two nodes, of which only 22,418 complete their plan). In the 60 s session, cap-reached runs exit with 3.96 planned client operations invoked and unanswered (invoked at median step 406) and about 2.4 further planned events never released behind them; the exempt merge removed the client-before-restart edges, but the write chain (max_concurrent_writes 2) and the density-0.3 edges still order later writes, reads and fault pairs after operations that target a node stuck in recovery, so those events wait until the cap. Settling the stuck operations lets the remaining events run on the two nodes that still serve requests (client_anchor census: the rest of the system answers; the loop is confined to the stuck node), which turns a cap-length stall into a run that finishes its plan a few hundred steps after the release and issues its remaining reads and writes into the post-fault state that Porcupine checks. Where a released successor is a crash pair the restart happens on a system that has been quiet, which is a fresh restart-and-delivery window. The size of the fault-side conversion is the uncertain quantity, so it is the firing floor: if fewer than 10,000 fault events per chunk are released the mechanism is a completion device only and is graded as such.
hypothesis.generalityArgument: The rule is a plan-graph liveness rule with no protocol content: no planned event waits on a client operation past the point where the run has provably stopped changing state. It reads only the engine's statuses and the run's progress marks. The invocation stays in the history without a response, which every linearizability model already treats as a pending operation, so the ground truth is unchanged for every panel member.

hypothesis.redTeam: The stalled runs are wedged by a protocol-state condition (a node stuck in recovering whose single Recovery is never retried, per the iteration-76 anatomy), not by a scheduling choice. Settling the stuck operations releases the write-chain and density successors, but the released client operations draw their destinations from the plan and can target the stuck node again, so many released runs wedge a second time a few steps later; on the exempt half (by workload seed) RecoverNode events already have no client predecessors, so the fault conversion pool is confined to the stock half's 71,637 unrecovered crashes per chunk. The released runs are longer, so the release cell is unbalanced on steps per run against the cut cell and, by the iteration-76 precedent, the grader will read it cross-binary against a cache that now already contains the parent; the candidate's cross-binary band and cost clause were written against a pre-merge baseline and would close it spuriously. Late responses above 3% would indict the parent's premise as much as this child.

The fault-conversion floor is grounded: plan_deps.stock.density_positive.unrecovered_crashes 71,637 and zero_recovery_runs 21,157 on the stock half sit behind client operations, which is what this release un-blocks. One mechanism family with the merged stall cap and with stall-release-of-withheld-faults; this goes first. Bit 1<<12 (4096, retired recoverWindowFreshOnly) is free and uncontested. reviewSummary: Nine candidates, none rejected. All verification is against the merged tree (spur 3d88510) and its fresh baseline 819d3a0bf347 (seeds 1000/1001). Stall-point family: stall-release-of-client-blocked-plan-events and stall-release-of-withheld-faults are one mechanism family at the same exit (path.rs:1047-1081); the client-blocked release supersedes the withheld-faults release as a standalone because it releases both client and fault successors and keeps issuing client operations after the release (a violation needs a client observation), while the withheld-faults release cannot issue a client operation and cannot reach plan completion in wedged runs (its plan_complete clauses were false as reasoned and are removed). Order: client-blocked first; withheld-faults re-enters as a nested force-faults addition. Both lengthen runs and are read cross-binary against the merged cache with an internal preservation guard; the client-blocked candidate's cross-binary band and cost clause were written against the pre-merge baseline and are re-based. stalled-runs-admitted-as-replay-prefix-parents is classified as an enabling change (a new parent source), not a retired replay-prefix ranking rule, but as written it shares the 64-slot ring with the signal parents and would displace them about 4:1, and the recorded stall anatomy says the wedge is a protocol-state condition the suffix cannot leave; rewritten to require a separate ring and a supply guard. run-cap-headroom-one-dose rests on numbers the iteration-76 merge invalidated (295,328 cap-reached runs, cap 3,275: now 136,951 and 3,887/4,031); re-based at the floor. replay-parent-served-by-child-arm-set: stock fidelity is now 0.50-0.52, not 0.43-0.50; the rung read is under-powered by its own note. run-local counters: every counter identity verified exactly; cost 2 for rewriting the accounting layer other candidates' firing floors depend on. Bits: 1<<12 (client-blocked release), 1<<25 (withheld faults), 1<<26 (crash restart window), 1<<27 (stall parents), 1<<22/1<<23 (arm-set serving), 1<<11/1<<17 (PCT), 1<<16 (headroom) are all retired rows with no tag in run_variant.rs and no two candidates claim the same bit. Checkable claims found false: withheld-faults' plan-completion reachability; headroom's cap-reached population and current cap on the merged tree; client-blocked release's cross-binary band relative to a baseline that now contains its parent.

otherCandidates.scoreReason: A new direction on the crash-timing axis with every code claim verified: crash_hold_mask at core/scheduler.rs:703, SendLedger with in_flight, entries_at_restart, net_fresh and ghost_acted_since_restart at core/state.rs:731-748, entries_since_restart at state.rs:1161, fault_timing::draw_hold at 187 and cap_reserve at 178, crash_phase::WINDOW = 96. The hold is bounded (WINDOW / cap_reserve) so it reads on the internal per-run rung, as required. The generality statement names no handler or role and reuses ledger counters every protocol maintains. The rationale's headline statistic is loosely matched to the predicate (see red team), which costs evidence credit; the causal story to depth 8 is asserted rather than demonstrated. Bit 1<<26 (67108864, retired originAlternate) is free and uncontested. Implementation constraint: the new hold must extend crash_hold_until or otherwise count as suspended in exec_plan's stall clock (path.rs:1036-1046), or the merged stall cap cuts a held run as stalled.
otherCandidates.redTeam: The evidence cited for the window being common (recoveries_with_own_prior_sends_inflight 1,112,223 of 1,516,908) measures the restarting node's PRE-crash ghost sends still in flight at its recovery, not post-restart fresh sends undelivered, which is the condition the hold keys on; the two are different populations and the second is unmeasured. Post-restart fresh sends are the restart's own fan-out and deliver within a handful of steps, so the window is open briefly after each restart; a crash whose placement step arrives before any peer has restarted waits its bounded 96 steps and expires to stock, so landed_in_window/armed at 0.55 is optimistic. The record already holds cascade-fault-window-admission (rejected: crashes inside another node's fresh-restart window steered toward a zero-violation stratum on this 3-node rig) and crash-hold-while-peer-restart-unsettled (held: a hold on a peer's recovery progress expires by construction on the rung's chain); this arm keys on the opposite predicate but the crash still lands while a peer is mid-recovery, and depth 8 asks for the recovered peer to receive the initiating node's Recovery, which a fresh crash of a third node does not obviously produce. Placed-crash runs already carry the phase arms, so the hold composes with the phase wait and the combined wait may exhaust the cap reserve.
